content: In all prevalence settings, the use of Strategies B and, if on-site RPR testing is available, Strategy C, results in approximately 4 additional treatments per 1,000 pregnant women in low-prevalence settings and 20–30 additional treatments per 1,000 in higher-prevalence settings. The difference in harms related to over-treatment between a single on-site rapid syphilis test (RST, Strategy A) and a single on-site rapid plasma reagin (RPR, Strategy B) test is minimal in low-prevalence settings, with 9 more cases of over-treatment per 1,000 pregnant women using the RPR strategy. However, in higher-prevalence settings, the difference in over-treatment between these two strategies is moderate, favoring the RST strategy, with approximately 30–50 fewer cases of over-treatment per 1,000 women compared to the RPR strategy. The difference in over-treatment between the on-site RST followed by RPR (Strategy C) and the single on-site RPR test (Strategy B) is negligible. Similarly, the difference in harms related to missed treatment is small between the single on-site RST (Strategy A) and the single on-site RPR test (Strategy B) in low-prevalence settings, with approximately 4 more missed cases per 1,000 women using the RPR strategy. However, in higher-prevalence settings, the difference is moderate, with 25–30 more missed cases per 1,000 women using the RPR strategy. The number of pregnant women screened appears to be slightly higher with the single on-site RST strategy (Strategy A) but is otherwise similar across other strategies and prevalence settings. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) emphasized the importance of prioritizing missed cases of syphilis due to the severe adverse effects of untreated syphilis during pregnancy, including the risks of congenital syphilis and fetal death. While over-treatment may result in minor side effects, such as gastrointestinal symptoms, it is considered acceptable in some cases. However, over-treatment in large proportions of tested women is undesirable. Although there is no direct evidence on the impact of different screening and treatment strategies on partner notification, the GDG agreed that providing a sequence of tests (Strategy C) could increase partner treatment by enhancing confidence in positive results among tested women and their partners. Cost-effectiveness modeling indicates that the total costs per 1,000 women screened are lowest with RPR in Tanzania and Zambia, while RST is the cheapest option in Peru due to labor costs associated with RPR. The most cost-effective approach across all prevalence settings is the single on-site RST followed by treatment if positive (Strategy A), although this strategy may incur higher costs in some settings. The GDG agreed that a single on-site RST followed by treatment (Strategy A) or an on-site RST followed by a first dose of treatment and subsequent RPR testing (Strategy C) may result in more people being treated, fewer missed cases, and fewer incidents of over-treatment compared to other strategies (e.g., Strategy B). In low-prevalence settings, Strategies A and C yield similar results, while in higher-prevalence settings, fewer women are over-treated with Strategy C. The single on-site RST strategy (Strategy A) is cost-effective, feasible to implement, and acceptable to key stakeholders. However, in resource-constrained settings, a sequence of on-site tests may be unaffordable and require adequate provider training. On-site tests have been successfully implemented in many countries, demonstrating their feasibility. The GDG recommends that healthcare providers receive training and information about syphilis prevalence in pregnant women and the risks of mother-to-fetus transmission. Pregnant women and their partners may require additional support when discussing partner treatment. Monitoring and evaluation of these strategies are essential, and further research is needed to compare the sensitivity and specificity of different test sequences, as well as their long-term outcomes for mothers and infants.
